chains.earliest_control: a DMARC enforcement policy in force (p=quarantine, then p=reject once the aggregate reports allow)
chains.name: Spoofed invoice

steps.text: The firm bills clients by email from its own domain (D4); a client and an invoice cycle are easy to learn.

An attacker sends a payment-change email as the firm to a client. The SPF record ends in a soft fail and DMARC is at p=none (DNS-EM-02, DNS-EM-04; D1, D5), so receivers apply no enforcement and the message delivers as genuine.
The client pays the next invoice to the attacker's account.

chains.earliest_control: dangling records to deprovisioned services removed
chains.name: Subdomain takeover

steps.text: help.wrenfield.example still points at the helpdesk service the firm left in 2024, which answers that no site is configured for the name (DNS-SUB-02; F2).
An attacker opens an account at the helpdesk service and claims that name, so the firm's own subdomain serves the attacker's page.
A credential-harvesting page answers on a subdomain of the firm's real domain, and clients and staff trust the name.

chains.earliest_control: registry lock, so the domain cannot be changed until the lock is removed
chains.name: Registrar social engineering

steps.text: An attacker calls the registrar's support desk posing as the firm. The account's recovery contact is a departed staff member's personal mailbox (DNS-REG-01; A1), so the firm sees none of the support desk's notices.
The support desk changes the domain's nameservers. With no registry lock (DNS-REG-03; A2) nothing holds the change until a lock is removed, and it takes effect.
The attacker's zone points the domain's mail at the attacker, and the firm's mail is rerouted for a weekend before anyone notices.
